issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination appraisals are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another person; for this trauma type, guilt, responsibility, danger, or moral failure would be more coherent than feeling physically dirty/contaminated, absent any assault or bodily violation context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: Other-blame rumination conflicts with the trauma type and the rest of the profile: the central event is that he accidentally injured another person, while the appraisals emphasize defectiveness and threat rather than victimization by others. Dwelling on what other people have done to me points to a different trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: Magical thinking that the event did not really happen or was not that bad sits awkwardly with the very high-severity profile and with simultaneous endorsement of full sensory reliving plus strong persistent threat and self-defectiveness. Partial minimization can occur, but this item as phrased is in notable tension with the rest of the profile.

vignette: Rajiv had always taken pride in his work as a Coast Guard officer, believing he was making a difference in the lives of others. However, a fateful day two years ago shattered that sense of purpose. During a routine training exercise, he accidentally caused a life-threatening injury to a fellow officer. The incident replayed in his mind like a film reel stuck on a single scene, the sound of sirens piercing through the air as he rushed to assist, the panic and chaos overshadowing everything else. Now, at eighty years old, Rajiv found himself haunted by fragmented memories, pieces that would come and go without warning. He struggled to recall details deliberately, often feeling as if the memory was just out of reach, leaving him with an overwhelming sense of confusion and guilt. Since the accident, Rajiv’s world had become increasingly constricted. He avoided nature walks near the shoreline—the very place where the incident had occurred. Whenever he ventured into outdoor spaces reminiscent of that fateful day, an acute sense of danger enveloped him, making it hard to breathe. The trees swayed in the wind, and the birds chirped cheerfully, but all he could hear were the sirens, a ghostly reminder that he was partly responsible for someone else’s pain. The sound and sights of nature triggered vivid memories of the incident, pulling him back into that chaotic moment and amplifying the sense of guilt that he carried with him. Each time he stepped outside, he felt as if he were treading on fragile ground, his hypervigilance compelling him to scan every shadow, every rustle, for signs of impending danger. This constant state of alertness gnawed at him, convincing him that he needed to stay on guard at all times. Each time he felt that familiar sense of danger, it heightened his awareness of potential threats, making even the smallest noise feel like a warning of impending disaster. The world outside his home felt unpredictable, and he had come to believe that it was safer to remain within the confines of familiar places. Rajiv’s self-perception had also taken a significant hit since the accident. He often thought to himself, "There’s something wrong with me." He was convinced that the incident was a reflection of his character—that he was somehow flawed or defective. Every time he faced reminders of the accident, it reinforced his negative self-perception, leading him to believe that he was unworthy of safety or happiness. This negative appraisal weighed heavily on him, feeding into a cycle of maladaptive strategies. To cope, he forced himself to think only positive thoughts, denying the reality of what had transpired. This strategy of denial only deepened his negative beliefs, as he began to feel that if he couldn’t accept what happened, it confirmed that he was incapable of facing his emotions. In his mind, he told himself the event didn’t really happen or wasn’t that bad, as if by suppressing the truth, he could wash away the guilt. He struggled to recall details deliberately, often feeling as if the memory was just out of reach, leaving him with an overwhelming sense of confusion and guilt. Since the accident, Rajiv’s world had become increasingly constricted. He avoided nature walks near the shoreline—the very place where the incident had occurred. Whenever he ventured into outdoor spaces reminiscent of that fateful day, an acute sense of danger enveloped him, making it hard to breathe. The trees swayed in the wind, and the birds chirped cheerfully, but all he could hear were the sirens, a ghostly reminder that he was partly responsible for someone else’s pain. The sound and sights of nature triggered vivid memories of the incident, pulling him back into that chaotic moment and amplifying the sense of guilt that he carried with him. Each time he stepped outside, he felt as if he were treading on fragile ground, his hypervigilance compelling him to scan every shadow, every rustle, for signs of impending danger. This constant state of alertness gnawed at him, convincing him that he needed to stay on guard at all times. Each time he felt that familiar sense of danger, it heightened his awareness of potential threats, making even the smallest noise feel like a warning of impending disaster. The world outside his home felt unpredictable, and he had come to believe that it was safer to remain within the confines of familiar places. Rajiv’s self-perception had also taken a significant hit since the accident. He often thought to himself, "There’s something wrong with me." He was convinced that the incident was a reflection of his character—that he was somehow flawed or defective. Every time he faced reminders of the accident, it reinforced his negative self-perception, leading him to believe that he was unworthy of safety or happiness.
